newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street urges caution on electric deregulation.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street urges caution on electric deregulation.

text.p: Wall Street analysts and electric utility investors Thursday urged Congress to let states move to deregulate local power markets at their own pace and ensure the industry remains financially stable.

Analysts warned that if customers who stopped buying power from their local utility in an open market were let off the hook from paying for investments made to serve them, then utility shareholders would be left carrying the burden.

"The market for these stocks would crater," if utilities were blocked from recovering their stranded costs, Morgan Stanley & Co principal Kit Kotolidge said at a Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee workshop.
A study by Resource Data International Inc estimated total stranded costs for utilities, including generation assets and high-priced power purchase contracts, at $202 billion.
"It would not be good policy to bankrupt these major energy providers," said Douglas Kimmelman, a managing director of Goldman, Sachs & Co.

If shareholders have to carry stranded costs, investors might shy away from the industry, which would hike the costs of raising capital, and in turn could result in higher, not lower rates, for utility customers, said Kotolidge.
"Attempts to drastically and suddenly lower investors' returns during the transition period could have the perverse effect of increasing the price of electricity in the future," he said.
Following the line utilities have been advocating, investor advisors said states should be left in charge of deciding how to resolve the stranded cost issue.

"Those individuals involved with the original decisions related to utility rate levels are best-suited to strike a proper balance (between shareholders and customers) on stranded cost recovery," said Steven Fetter, senior diretor of Fitch Investors Service, LP.

Uncertainty over the future of the industry has brought the average electric utility stock down about 13 percent since 1993 at the same time that the broader stock market has climbed more than 70 percent, Kotolidge said.
The people hurt most by the decline represent the bulk of utility investors -- older, retired people who are dependent on stable dividends, said Frank Pazlar, chairman of Minnesota Utility Investors.
